case.title: GET latency regression after gateway 5.8 at Tarnfield Object Storage
case.setting: Quillon Cloud runs Tarnfield, a fictional object storage service. Stateless gateways terminate client requests, check request signatures, look up metadata and fetch object chunks from storage nodes. The fleet is organised as 12 cells across three regions (us-e, ap-s, eu-w). Gateway software ships through a release pipeline that posts to a shared change calendar. Storage-node settings are changed through a separate fleet configuration system.
case.presentingRequest: The VP of Platform Engineering wants a decision today on rolling gateway 5.8 back to 5.7 across the fleet. You have been asked to assess what is driving the GET latency regression and which of the proposed actions should be taken. You may collect at most two items from the catalogue.

initialEvidence.source: Priya Halvorsen, VP Platform Engineering, email to incident channel, 4 Nov 09:12
initialEvidence.text: GET p99 has been stuck near 300 ms since the gateway 5.8 rollout on the night of 2–3 Nov. Before that it was 90 ms. The dashboard shows it climbing as the rollout went out. 5.8 changed the read path, and gateway CPU is up 18%. I want a fleet-wide rollback to 5.7 today. Security has objected because of the signature fix, but customer latency comes first and we can re-ship the fix later. The storage and network teams have confirmed nothing of theirs is involved.

initialEvidence.source: Fleet latency dashboard export with deployment annotations
initialEvidence.text: Fleet GET p99, hourly average of 5-minute p99 values (ms), night of 2–3 Nov. Annotation: 'gateway 5.8 rollout 22:05–04:10 (us-e 22:05–23:30, ap-s 23:35–01:50, eu-w 02:30–04:10)'. 20:00 90; 21:00 91; 22:00 93; 23:00 139; 00:00 284; 01:00 291; 02:00 296; 03:00 301; 04:00 298; 05:00 297. Daily median p99: 1 Nov 90, 2 Nov 91, 4 Nov 296, 6 Nov 294, 8 Nov 297. The shared change calendar for 2–3 Nov has one entry: gateway 5.8 rollout.

Changes: (1) Fixes SEC-2291, a request-signature replay weakness reported by external auditors. Versions 5.7 and earlier remain exposed, and audit closure requires 5.8 across the fleet by 30 Nov. (2) Read path: parallel range-fetch fan-out raised from 4 to 8 for large objects. (3) TLS library upgrade. Known effect: gateway CPU +15–20% from the added signature checks. Rollback procedure: redeploy 5.7, about 4 hours across the fleet.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, storage platform manager, 4 Nov
initialEvidence.text: 'We pushed a routine compaction tuning change through the fleet config system on the evening of 2 Nov, because backlog alerts had been firing since about 31 Oct. Fleet config pushes don't go on the shared change calendar and never have. Compaction is background work and yields to client reads, so it can't be behind a read-latency problem. And to be clear, we never pause compaction. Once backlog passes about 15% of extents, read amplification climbs and nodes start running toward disk-full.'

'Elevated TCP retransmits on us-e spine-2 from 02:10 to 04:50 on 3 Nov, traced to a flapping optic. We replaced the optic at 04:50 and retransmits have been at baseline since. Nothing comparable in ap-s or eu-w. Gateway-to-storage round-trip time medians are 0.4–0.6 ms in all three regions, same as last week. We don't see a network angle on the GET latency issue.'

initialEvidence.source: Customer success note and traffic summary, 4 Nov
initialEvidence.text: On 30 Oct Orrin Media began migrating its archive into Tarnfield, writing about 18 TB/day across all three regions. It is a background copy with a 15 Dec deadline and is currently ahead of schedule. Orrin's contract allows temporary ingest rate limits with 24 hours' notice, and their technical lead has said pacing is fine. Fleet traffic, 28 Oct to 4 Nov: GET requests/s rose 6%, gradually across the week. PUT requests/s rose 14%.

catalogue.title: Gateway 5.8 code review record and test summary
catalogue.text: Code review record, GW-5.8. 41 merged changes, each with two approvals. Unit and integration suites passed (2,318 tests). The range-fetch fan-out change applies to objects above 64 MiB. The signature check adds an HMAC verification and a nonce-cache lookup per request. Reviewer comment: 'possible CPU cost; no storage-side effect expected.' Integration tests run against an in-memory storage stub, not real storage nodes.

catalogue.title: Pre-release staging load test results, gateway 5.7 vs 5.8
catalogue.text: Pre-release load test, staging, 28 Oct. 40-minute runs at 70% of production peak GET rate, first gateway 5.7 then 5.8, against six staging storage nodes holding synthetic data (about 2% of production volume, lightly loaded). GET p99: 5.7 84 ms, 5.8 87 ms. Gateway CPU: 5.7 31%, 5.8 37%. Test owner's note: 'staging storage is not representative of production disk load; treat storage-side numbers as indicative only.'

catalogue.title: Customer support tickets mentioning latency, 3–8 Nov
catalogue.text: Support queue extract, 3–8 Nov. 64 tickets mention slow downloads or timeouts, from 41 accounts across all three regions. 11 cite SDK timeouts at 250 ms. Two enterprise accounts asked for an incident declaration and confirmation of SLA credits. Agents tagged 52 tickets 'gateway 5.8' after the internal status note named the release. No ticket pins down when the slowness started more precisely than 'overnight on the 2nd'.

catalogue.title: Gateway host metrics (CPU, memory, connection pools), 1–8 Nov
catalogue.text: Gateway fleet metrics, 1–8 Nov. CPU median 34% before 2 Nov, 40% after. Peak 52% (previously 44%). Memory flat. In-use connections from gateways to storage nodes rose from about 1,900 to about 5,800 per region overnight on 2–3 Nov. The pool limit is 8,000, with no exhaustion events. Gateway request queue depth was zero throughout, and no gateway host exceeded 60% CPU.

catalogue.title: Distributed trace sample, GET requests, 3 Nov
catalogue.text: Trace sample, 3 Nov 10:00–10:20: 40 GET traces from us-e, all served by gateway 5.8. Median span times: authentication and signature check 4 ms. Metadata lookup 6 ms. Storage fetch 271 ms (gateway-side span, includes network and storage-node time). Response streaming 12 ms. Traces are kept for 24 hours, so there are no pre-release traces to compare against.

Orrin's tooling copies it via PUT at a target of 18 TB/day across us-e, ap-s and eu-w, in proportion to Orrin's existing footprint. Started 30 Oct, completion target 15 Dec. On 7 Nov progress was 9% ahead of plan. Orrin does not expect to read migrated data before January.

catalogue.text: 'The fan-out change only applies to objects over 64 MiB, which is about 3% of GETs. The signature check costs CPU, not much latency: we measured 1–2 ms in staging. I don't see how 5.8 adds 200 ms to fleet p99, but I can't rule it out until someone shows me a cell where the timing doesn't line up. Rolling back hurts us too: the SEC-2291 audit deadline is 30 Nov and 5.7 is still exposed.'

catalogue.title: Storage-node host and compaction metrics, 28 Oct–8 Nov
catalogue.text:
Storage observability export, 28 Oct–8 Nov. Node medians across the 11 cells that applied FC-7710.
Compaction worker threads: 2 before the push, 6 after.
Compaction share of disk bytes: 38% before, 71% after.
Disk utilisation: 41% before, 97% after. It crossed 90% within 5 minutes of the push in each of the 11 cells.
Disk read queue wait: 9 ms before, 205 ms after.

initialEvidence.text: GET p99 has been stuck near 300 ms since the gateway 5.8 rollout on the night of 2–3 Nov. Before that it was 90 ms. Storage-node settings are changed through a separate fleet configuration system.
case.presentingRequest: The VP of Platform Engineering wants a decision today on rolling gateway 5.8 back to 5.7 across the fleet. You have been asked to assess what is driving the GET latency regression and which of the proposed actions should be taken. You may collect at most two items from the catalogue.

initialEvidence.source: Priya Halvorsen, VP Platform Engineering, email to incident channel, 4 Nov 09:12
initialEvidence.text: GET p99 has been stuck near 300 ms since the gateway 5.8 rollout on the night of 2–3 Nov. Before that it was 90 ms. The dashboard shows it climbing as the rollout went out. 5.8 changed the read path, and gateway CPU is up 18%. I want a fleet-wide rollback to 5.7 today. Security has objected because of the signature fix, but customer latency comes first and we can re-ship the fix later. The storage and network teams have confirmed nothing of theirs is involved.

initialEvidence.source: Fleet latency dashboard export with deployment annotations
initialEvidence.text: Fleet GET p99, hourly average of 5-minute p99 values (ms), night of 2–3 Nov. Annotation: 'gateway 5.8 rollout 22:05–04:10 (us-e 22:05–23:30, ap-s 23:35–01:50, eu-w 02:30–04:10)'. 20:00 90; 21:00 91; 22:00 93; 23:00 139; 00:00 284; 01:00 291; 02:00 296; 03:00 301; 04:00 298; 05:00 297. Daily median p99: 1 Nov 90, 2 Nov 91, 4 Nov 296, 6 Nov 294, 8 Nov 297. The shared change calendar for 2–3 Nov has one entry: gateway 5.8 rollout.

Changes: (1) Fixes SEC-2291, a request-signature replay weakness reported by external auditors. Versions 5.7 and earlier remain exposed, and audit closure requires 5.8 across the fleet by 30 Nov. (2) Read path: parallel range-fetch fan-out raised from 4 to 8 for large objects. (3) TLS library upgrade. Known effect: gateway CPU +15–20% from the added signature checks. Rollback procedure: redeploy 5.7, about 4 hours across the fleet.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, storage platform manager, 4 Nov
initialEvidence.text: 'We pushed a routine compaction tuning change through the fleet config system on the evening of 2 Nov, because backlog alerts had been firing since about 31 Oct. Fleet config pushes don't go on the shared change calendar and never have. Compaction is background work and yields to client reads, so it can't be behind a read-latency problem. And to be clear, we never pause compaction. Once backlog passes about 15% of extents, read amplification climbs and nodes start running toward disk-full.'

'Elevated TCP retransmits on us-e spine-2 from 02:10 to 04:50 on 3 Nov, traced to a flapping optic. We replaced the optic at 04:50 and retransmits have been at baseline since. Nothing comparable in ap-s or eu-w. Gateway-to-storage round-trip time medians are 0.4–0.6 ms in all three regions, same as last week. We don't see a network angle on the GET latency issue.'

initialEvidence.source: Customer success note and traffic summary, 4 Nov
initialEvidence.text: On 30 Oct Orrin Media began migrating its archive into Tarnfield, writing about 18 TB/day across all three regions. It is a background copy with a 15 Dec deadline and is currently ahead of schedule. Orrin's contract allows temporary ingest rate limits with 24 hours' notice, and their technical lead has said pacing is fine. Fleet traffic, 28 Oct to 4 Nov: GET requests/s rose 6%, gradually across the week. PUT requests/s rose 14%.

catalogue.text: Code review record, GW-5.8. 41 merged changes, each with two approvals. Unit and integration suites passed (2,318 tests). The range-fetch fan-out change applies to objects above 64 MiB. The signature check adds an HMAC verification and a nonce-cache lookup per request. Reviewer comment: 'possible CPU cost; no storage-side effect expected.' Integration tests run against an in-memory storage stub, not real storage nodes.

catalogue.title: Pre-release staging load test results, gateway 5.7 vs 5.8
catalogue.text: Pre-release load test, staging, 28 Oct. 40-minute runs at 70% of production peak GET rate, first gateway 5.7 then 5.8, against six staging storage nodes holding synthetic data (about 2% of production volume, lightly loaded). GET p99: 5.7 84 ms, 5.8 87 ms. Gateway CPU: 5.7 31%, 5.8 37%. Test owner's note: 'staging storage is not representative of production disk load; treat storage-side numbers as indicative only.'

catalogue.text: Support queue extract, 3–8 Nov. 64 tickets mention slow downloads or timeouts, from 41 accounts across all three regions. 11 cite SDK timeouts at 250 ms. truth.groundTruthNarrative: The GET latency regression was caused by storage fleet config change FC-7710. Between 23:38 and 23:52 on 2 Nov it raised compaction worker threads from 2 to 6 on storage nodes in 11 of the 12 cells. Gateway 5.8 happened to be rolling out over the same night (22:05–04:10). Leadership, the hourly fleet dashboard, the shared change calendar (which never lists fleet config pushes) and a prior incident precedent all pointed at the release. The per-cell export breaks the coincidence. In every pushed cell, latency rose within minutes of that cell's push, even in seven cells that did not get 5.8 until later. Cell aps-3 had 5.8 from 01:05 and comparable traffic growth, but its push was skipped by a maintenance freeze, and it stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 for three hours changed nothing. Storage-node metrics give the mechanism. Compaction's share of disk bytes rose from 38% to 71% and utilisation from 41% to 97%. Disk read queue wait rose by about 196 ms, which matches the increase in node-side GET service time and p99. Network transport was unaffected. Why the backlog grew before 2 Nov (Orrin's migration writes, a lifecycle-expiry sweep, or both) is unresolved. The best next step is a staged, monitored revert of the compaction change. Rolling back the gateway would re-open the SEC-2291 security weakness with no latency benefit. Pausing compaction for weeks would push backlog past the 15% danger threshold.

answers.rationale: C6 shows the regression began in each cell within minutes of that cell's FC-7710 push, before 5.8 arrived in seven cells. aps-3 ran 5.8 from 01:05 without the push and stayed at 91→94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 for three hours left p99 unchanged (291/297/293). The release does not covary with the regression, and removing it does not help. The rollout alignment in E1 and E2 is a coincidence in timing.

E4 places a compaction tuning change on the evening of 2 Nov. C6 shows onset in every pushed cell 2–13 minutes after its push, regardless of gateway version. The one cell without the push (aps-3, hardware unchanged, similar traffic) did not regress. C11 adds the disk-saturation mechanism. The storage manager's claim that compaction 'can't' affect reads is an interested assertion, and the data contradict it.

Traffic rose gradually (GET +6% over a week; E6), but latency stepped up within minutes in each cell (E2, C6). aps-3 saw comparable GET growth (+7%) and kept its baseline latency. Traffic growth without the config push did not produce the regression.

Retransmits were confined to us-e between 02:10 and 04:50. That is after the regression began at about 23:40 (E2), and the regression persisted after the optic was replaced and appeared in regions with no network anomaly. Gateway-to-storage RTT was unchanged at 0.4–0.6 ms. C11 confirms the added time is on the storage node, excluding network.

Several pieces of evidence count against the link itself: 5.8 present without the regression (aps-3), the regression present before 5.8 arrived (aps-2 and all eu-w cells), and a rollback with no effect (euw-1, 6 Nov). This goes beyond a rival being supported: the release itself is shown not to drive the regression.

C11 shows compaction threads tripled at the push. Compaction's share of disk bytes rose from 38% to 71%, and utilisation went from 41% to 97%, crossing 90% within 5 minutes of the push in each of the 11 cells. Temporal order, mechanism and attribution of the extra disk load to compaction establish the link. No other catalogue item has disk data.

C11: disk read queue wait rose by 196 ms (9→205), matching the rise in node-side service time (61→262 ms) and in cell p99 (about +200 ms). C6 rules out the main rival (the gateway release) and shows that the one unpushed cell did not regress. E5 rules out the network. Temporal order, mechanism and covariation, with the rival excluded, make the link causal.

The backlog grew from 3.1% to 11.2% while Orrin's migration writes were running (from 30 Oct). Over the same period a lifecycle-expiry sweep (29 Oct–1 Nov) was writing deletion markers that compaction must process. C11 states that the backlog has not been attributed by source or node. The two co-occur, but the competing driver is not ruled out.

The rollback test in C6 shows 5.7 gives no latency benefit, and H1 is contradicted, so no live hypothesis is served by the rollback. It would re-expose the fleet to the SEC-2291 signature-replay weakness and put the 30 Nov audit closure at risk (E3). It removes a protective security fix for no gain.

The evidence identifies the compaction change as the cause. A one-cell-first revert is reversible (C8: takes effect within 5 minutes). Monitoring backlog guards against the read-amplification risk in E4, and the backlog is now 4.0% (C11), well below 15%. This is the single best next action.

Pacing Orrin's ingest would help keep the backlog down if Orrin's writes drive it (R4), but that link is only an association, and the lifecycle sweep is an unexcluded rival. The contract permits temporary rate limits with notice, the migration is ahead of schedule and the customer accepts pacing (E6, C9), so a wrong call leaves no lasting damage. It is not justified yet.

Compaction is a protective process. At the old 2-thread setting the backlog grew about 8 points in 4 days (C11), so with compaction stopped for one to two weeks it would pass the 15% threshold. Past that point read amplification raises GET latency and nodes head toward disk-full (E4). A short-term latency gain turns into a worse outcome.

The CPU increase is real (E3, C4) and worth understanding for capacity planning. It is low cost and harmless, but C6 shows 5.8 is not behind the regression, so this does nothing for the incident. Reasonable, but not among the best next actions.

The top-ranked substantive action is the staged revert of the compaction change (A2). It rests on a natural experiment (aps-3), onset matching each cell's push time, a negative rollback test, and a disk-saturation mechanism whose size matches the regression. That is enough to commit to a reversible, monitored revert.

truth.authoringNotes: Misleading signal: the hourly fleet dashboard (E2) and the VP (E1) tie the regression to the gateway 5.8 rollout. The release notes (E3) list a read-path change and higher CPU, the change calendar lists only the release, and the storage manager (E4) dismisses compaction as unable to affect reads. From the initial file alone, a careful analyst would likely mark H1 supported or unknown, H2 unknown, R1 association-only, R2/R3 unknown, A1 preferred or premature, A2 premature and SUFF insufficient. E2 holds a fair but non-decisive hint: the 22:00 hour stays at 93 ms even though us-e cells had 5.8 from 22:05. Non-redundancy: C6 alone settles H1, R1 and A1, with its per-cell timing, the aps-3 natural experiment and the euw-1 rollback test. No other item has per-cell latency or a version comparison. C11 alone settles R2 (disk saturation attributed to compaction); no other item has disk data. R3 needs both. Other items are plausible but non-decisive. C4 (connection growth) and C5 (post-release traces, no baseline) fit either story. C8 states the change but not its effect. C10 is an interested and inconclusive account. C12 is a misleading base rate. C7 only repeats E5. aps-3 is a clean control: its freeze was for a future disk swap with hardware unchanged, it got 5.8 through the separate release pipeline, and its traffic growth is comparable. Only A2 is preferred. A1 is harmful because H1 is contradicted and the rollback re-opens SEC-2291. A3 is premature because R4 is association-only and pacing is contractually allowed and reversible. A4 is harmful because it disables a protective process for weeks.
